subject: general-mathematics
title: Logarithms
summary: What a logarithm is, how it links to indices, and the three laws.

lesson.text: A logarithm answers the question: what power do I raise the base to, to get this number? Since 10^2 = 100, the logarithm of 100 to base 10 is 2. We write log₁₀ 100 = 2.
If a^x = N, then log_a N = x. The two say exactly the same thing.

items: 10^0 = 1 means log₁₀ 1 = 0 (the log of 1 is 0 in any base)

lesson.text: They come straight from the laws of indices.

items: Product: log a + log b = log (ab)
Quotient: log a − log b = log (a ÷ b)
Power: log a^n = n log a

lesson.text: log a + log b is NOT log (a + b). That mistake costs marks every year.

questions.explanation: a^x = N becomes log_a N = x. Here a = 10, x = 3, N = 1000: log₁₀ 1000 = 3.
Product law: log₁₀ (4 × 25) = log₁₀ 100 = 2. log₁₀ 29 adds the numbers instead of multiplying.
7^0 = 1, so log₇ 1 = 0. The log of 1 is 0 in every base.
Quotient law: log₃ (54 ÷ 2) = log₃ 27. 3^3 = 27, so the answer is 3.
